description:
NeuroVisio

NeuroVision is a research platform exploring how spaceflight-related ocular changes, fluid dynamics, and tissue mechanics can advance understanding of optic nerve health and future regeneration research.

My inspiration is deeply personal: my daughter lost an eye to retinoblastoma. Her journey gave me a dream—to contribute to scientific advances that may one day help restore vision. I created NeuroVision to bring space science, engineering, and neuroscience together toward that hope.
summary:
NeuroVision is a research and engineering platform exploring how spaceflight-related ocular changes, fluid dynamics, and tissue mechanics can inform questions about optic nerve health. It brings space science, engineering, and neuroscience together in four workspaces: Daily Check-in for organizing observations; Periodic Measurements for tracking entries over time; Relationship Explorer for visualizing example trends using synthetic records; and a CFD/FEA Workbench for exploring simplified fluid-flow and mechanical modeling.

The workbench demonstrates steady laminar flow in a rigid circular tube and a one-dimensional, homogeneous, linear-elastic mechanical proxy. These are educational engineering demonstrations, not anatomical simulations, clinical predictions, or validated optic nerve models. The prototype is not connected to medical devices or NASA systems; manual entries are user-entered and session-only.

NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) were identified as potential research sources, but their datasets are not yet integrated. Developed using Python, Jupyter Notebook, Gradio, and data-analysis and visualization tools, NeuroVision aims to support future exploration of spaceflight vision effects, optic nerve protection, and, longer term, regeneration research. Inspired by my daughter’s experience with retinoblastoma and the loss of an eye, I hope to contribute to scientific advances that may one day help restore vision.

NeuroVision is a research prototype with four workspaces: Daily Check-in, Periodic Measurements, Relationship Explorer, and a CFD/FEA Workbench. It organizes observations and explores relationships relevant to spaceflight-associated ocular changes.

The computational workbench demonstrates simplified engineering models: a rigid circular-tube fluid-flow approximation and a one-dimensional linear-elastic mechanical proxy. These are educational research tools, not anatomical simulations or clinical predictions.

The project was developed using Python, Jupyter Notebook, Gradio, and data-analysis and visualization tools. Its creative approach connects space science, engineering, and neuroscience toward future research on optic nerve protection and regeneration.

The prototype uses synthetic demonstration records and is not connected to NASA systems or medical devices. NASA OSDR and LSDA are identified as potential research resources; their datasets have not yet been integrated.
